newsitem.title: USA: Clinton signals displeasure on Israeli settlements.
newsitem.headline: Clinton signals displeasure on Israeli settlements.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton on Monday signalled displeasure with Israel's settlements policy, saying it had become obstacle in talks with the Palestinians on Israel's planned troop redeployment from the West Bank town of Hebron.

At a news conference with European Union officials, Clinton said talks between the Israelis and Palestinians on Hebron were at a "critical juncture" and urged Israel not to pursue a settlements policy that might impede an agreement.

"The talks are at a critical juncture...The situation is full of tension, and full of frustration," he said. "They've had an agreement within grasp, with very little difference on Hebron, for some time now. The time has come to make that agreement."

"I don't think that -- on the settlement issue -- that anything should be done which would in effect be seen as pre-empting the outcome of something they have already agreed...should be part of the final negotiations," he added.

Asked by a reporter whether he agreed with the assessment of some U.S. officials that the West Bank settlement issue had become an obstacle in the talks between the Israelis and Palestinians, Clinton replied: "Absolutely, absolutely."

Israeli-Palestinian tensions have flared in the last week over Israel's decision to grant financial benefits to Jewish settlers in the West Bank, the killing of two settlers by Arab gunmen and the fatal shooting of an Arab by a Jewish farmer.

Clinton's remarks echoed earlier comments from the White House spokesman, who said the United States found the latest Israeli stance on settlements "troubling" and added that it had complicated efforts to reach peace in the region.

White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry, asked about the U.S. reaction to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's efforts to help settlers, told reporters: "They are a complicating factor in the negotiations."

"While we have always said that we believe settlements are a complicating factor in the negotiations, we also believe that it is troubling to see sides pre-empt issues that are under discussion by taking positions," McCurry said.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat has reacted angrily to Israel's decision to grant financial benefits to West Bank settlers, describing the move as a timebomb.
About 130,000 Jews live in settlements scattered among the two million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, areas that were captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.
Under prodding from Washington, Israel and the PLO agreed to resume talks on Monday about long-delayed Israeli troop redeployment from Hebron.

In a related development, three former U.S. secretaries of state and five other former U.S. officials urged Netanyahu in a letter to refrain from expanding Jewish settlements in the West Bank and Gaza.

"We, therefore, urge you as prime minister of the state of Israel, just as we also urge all on the Arab side, not to take unilateral actions that would preclude a meaningful negotiated settlement and a comprehensive and lasting peace," said the letter, a copy of which an Israeli spokesman faxed to Reuters.

The letter was signed by former secretaries of state James Baker, Lawrence Eagleburger and Cyrus Vance along with former senior officials Zbigniew Brzezinski, Frank Carlucci, Brent Scowcroft, Richard Fairbanks and Robert Strauss.
